clergy

/KLUR-jee/ - the stress falls on KLUR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Clergy means the body of people ordained for religious duties.

The hospital keeps a rotating roster of clergy on call, so patients of any faith can ask for a chaplain at midnight.

Example

The new bishop's first act was practical: she surveyed the diocese's clergy and found that a third of its parishes shared a single overworked priest, so she began recruiting and training more.

Clergy is a collective noun for the ordained as a group — priests, ministers, rabbis, imams considered as a body. One person is a member of the clergy (or a cleric); the formal word for everyone else is the laity.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

priesthood: The priesthood is the ordained body of one specific tradition, especially one whose leaders are called priests. Clergy is the cross-faith collective — priests, ministers, rabbis, and imams considered together. Every priesthood belongs to the clergy, but the clergy is far wider.

ministry: Ministry names the profession or work of religious service — the calling itself, and sometimes the department that carries it out. Clergy names the people: the ordained men and women as a body. You enter the ministry; you join the clergy.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

laity: the members of a faith who are not ordained

laypeople: the plain word for members without religious office

Where it sits · how official the religious role is — worshippers → deacons → clergy

worshippers vs. clergy: Worshippers simply attend and take part; they hold no office at all, stopping far short of the clergy, who are formally ordained.

deacons vs. clergy: Deacons hold a recognized office and assist at services, but in many traditions they stop short of the clergy proper, whose members are fully ordained.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — clergie

Root — clergie: the learned, ordained class (Old French, from Greek kleros, 'a lot, an allotted portion')

Put it together

Put it together: Clergy resists peeling: it came into English whole, from Old French clergie. Behind that sits Greek kleros, 'a lot or allotted portion' — the ordained were the group whose allotted inheritance was God's service. And because they were for centuries the people trained to read and write, the same root produced a thoroughly secular relative: clerk.

Use the root in a new word: clerk

Use the root in a new word: clerk: The county clerk records every deed, license, and court filing in the district.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Clergy is the standard collective word for ordained religious leaders across faiths, common in journalism and law. For one person, say 'a member of the clergy,' 'a cleric,' or the tradition's own title — pastor, rabbi, imam. The formal word for everyone unordained is the laity.
